Presumption
prē-zŭmp´shŭn
n. (a taking beforehand; confidence without warrant; the sin of acting with a high hand)
Latin praesumptio, a taking in advance, from prae, before, and sumere, to take. The presumptuous man takes what has not been given him — a place, a licence, or an assurance.

Biblical Definition

Scripture treats presumption as sin with a raised hand. “But the soul that doeth ought presumptuously… the same reproacheth the LORD; and that soul shall be cut off from among his people” (Num 15:30). David prays against it by name: “Keep back thy servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me: then shall I be upright, and I shall be innocent from the great transgression” (Psa 19:13). The false prophet speaks “presumptuously” (Deu 18:22), and Peter's false teachers are “presumptuous are they, selfwilled, they are not afraid to speak evil of dignities” (2Pe 2:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines presumption as supposition of the truth or real existence of something without direct proof; blind or headstrong confidence; unreasonable adventurousness; arrogance; in theology, a groundless confidence in divine favour.

expand to see more

PRESUMPTION, n. Supposition of the truth or real existence of something without direct or positive proof of the fact, but grounded on circumstantial or probable evidence.

2. Strong probability; as, the fact is proved by presumption.

3. Blind or headstrong confidence; unreasonable adventurousness; as, it is presumption to attempt what cannot be accomplished.

4. Arrogance; as, presumption in a subordinate.

5. Unreasonable confidence in divine favor.

Key Scripture

Num 15:30 — "But the soul that doeth ought presumptuously, whether he be born in the land, or a stranger, the same reproacheth the LORD; and that soul shall be cut off from among his people."

Psa 19:13 — "Keep back thy servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me: then shall I be upright, and I shall be innocent from the great transgression."

2Pe 2:10 — "But chiefly them that walk after the flesh in the lust of uncleanness, and despise government. Presumptuous are they, selfwilled, they are not afraid to speak evil of dignities."

Deu 18:22 — "When a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken, but the prophet hath spoken it presumptuously: thou shalt not be afraid of him."

Jas 4:13 — "Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain:"

Modern Corruption

Presumption counterfeits faith so exactly that men are lost by it, and the difference is whether God has spoken.

expand to see more

Faith and presumption look identical from the outside: both are confident, both act without visible support, and both use religious language. The difference is single and decisive — faith rests on something God has said, and presumption rests on something a man has decided God will do. The devil's proposal on the pinnacle was presumption dressed in a psalm, and the Lord's answer named it: thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God. Israel at Kadesh supplies the plainest case: told not to go up, they went up presumptuously into the hill, and were beaten back — the same act that would have been faith the day before was presumption the day after the word changed.

Numbers 15:30 sets it against sin of ignorance, for which the chapter has just provided a sacrifice, and the presumptuous soul is cut off — the Hebrew is with a high hand. What distinguishes it is not the size of the offence but the posture: a hand raised against a known command. That is why David's prayer in Psalm 19:13 asks for restraint rather than pardon, and why he links it to dominion; presumptuous sins are the ones that take over, because a conscience that has once been overruled deliberately is easier to overrule next time.

The gentlest form of the sin is in James 4:13, and most Christians commit it weekly: today or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain — and James's objection is not to planning but to the missing clause, if the Lord will. Presumption in that key is simply the assumption of tomorrow, and the verse gives the reason it is unwarranted: ye know not what shall be on the morrow. The remedy is not anxiety but a sentence.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew zud (H2102), to boil up, act proudly, presume; yad ramah (H3027, H7311), with a high hand; Greek tolmetes (G5113), a daring one, presumptuous; authades (G829), selfwilled.

expand to see more

Hebrew zud (H2102) — to act presumptuously; Deuteronomy 17:12–13, 18:20, 18:22, Exodus 21:14.

Hebrew beyad ramah (H7311) — with a high hand, presumptuously; Numbers 15:30, 33:3; zed (H2086), proud; Psalm 19:13.

Greek tolmetes (G5113) — presumptuous, daring; 2 Peter 2:10 only, with authades (G829), selfwilled.

Usage

"“The soul that doeth ought presumptuously… reproacheth the LORD” — sin with a high hand."

"“Keep back thy servant also from presumptuous sins” — restraint asked for, not pardon."

"“We will go into such a city… and get gain” — the missing clause is if the Lord will."
